props.title: Time Bandits
props.initialSlug: Young boy joins time-traveling dwarves on wild quest

sections.content: **Time Bandits** (1981) stands as Terry Gilliam's masterful blend of dark fantasy and children's adventure, following a young boy who joins six time-traveling dwarfs stealing treasures across history. The film shares DNA with later reality-bending children's films like **Pan's Labyrinth** (2006) and **Coraline** (2009), but with Gilliam's signature Monty Python-esque absurdist humor. Its practical effects and handcrafted feel influenced fantasy filmmaking for decades, seen in works like **The NeverEnding Story** (1984) and **Labyrinth** (1986).

sections.content: The film's exploration of good vs. evil through historical figures prefigured later works like **Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure** (1989) and **Night at the Museum** (2006). But where those films played history for laughs, Time Bandits injects genuine darkness and philosophical weight. The ending, where evil literally explodes and (spoiler) kills the parents, remains one of the boldest conclusions in children's cinema, matching the narrative courage of **Return to Oz** (1985). SUBHEAD: The Golden Age of Practical Effects Fantasy

Time Bandits arrived during a revolutionary period for practical effects in fantasy cinema. Along with **The Thing** (1982) and **Legend** (1985), it showcased what could be achieved through practical magic before CGI dominated. The film's handmade quality - from the Supreme Being's floating head to the giant emerging from the sea - demonstrates why many modern filmmakers like **Guillermo del Toro** still champion practical effects over digital.
